title: Probability, Biostatistics & Experimental Design
description: Probability, estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, and design principles for biological and engineering experiments, with reproducibility and uncertainty at the center.

outcomes.description: Distinguish sampling variability from measurement error.
Choose an analysis matched to design and outcome.
Interpret confidence intervals, p-values, and effect sizes.
Design controls, replication, randomization, and blinding.
Create a labeled quantitative graph using an explicit scale and the units of the measured variables.

lesson_objectives.description: Use conditional probability and Bayes' rule.
Explain why a sample mean varies across repeated samples.
Interpret an interval as a procedure for repeated sampling.
Interpret p-values conditional on the null and analysis plan.
Account for multiplicity and distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work.
Use randomization and blocking to reduce confounding.
Assess model residuals and distinguish replication levels.
Distinguish an observed descriptive mean difference from evidence of a causal or population-level effect.
Calculate group sample means from replicate values and place their coordinates on a labeled linear graph.
Compute a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate at a stated time from event and censoring times.
Explain why censored observations must not be dropped or treated as events.
Compare two groups with an event rate per person-time and interpret a rate ratio and its limits as an estimate of a hazard ratio.
Calculate the family-wise error rate and the expected number of false positives across many independent tests.
Apply the Bonferroni correction and the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to a list of p-values and count the rejections each allows.
Choose between family-wise and false-discovery control for a study goal, and interpret an adjusted result correctly.
Compute a difference in means, its standard error and a 95% confidence interval, and interpret the interval.
Calculate a standardized effect size and explain how sample size changes precision but not the effect.
Predict the expected remeasurement of an extreme value under regression to the mean and evaluate study designs that guard against it.

lessons.title: Probability, distributions, and sampling
lessons.worked_example: If biological replicates have SD=12 units and n=9 independent samples, the standard error of the mean is 12/√9=4 units.

modules.title: Estimation, confidence intervals, and effect sizes

lessons.title: Estimation, confidence intervals, and effect sizes
lessons.worked_example: If an estimated treatment effect is 4.0 units with 95% CI [1.0, 7.0], the interval excludes zero under that model, but the effect's biological importance still requires context.

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and multiple comparisons
lessons.worked_example: If 20 independent null tests each use α=0.05 without correction, the probability of at least one false positive is 1−0.95²⁰≈0.64.

lessons.title: Experimental design, regression, and reproducibility
lessons.worked_example: In a 2-condition study across 6 independent donors, donor is a biological replication/blocking factor; measuring 100 cells per donor improves within-donor precision but does not create 600 independent donors.

modules.title: Descriptive evidence and limits of inference

lessons.title: Descriptive differences and inferential limits
lessons.worked_example: At 0, 2, and 4 μM, replicate signal means of 5, 10, and 15 form the plotted sample coordinates. Plotting the means preserves the dose order but hides within-group spread; it does not establish uncertainty or causation.

lessons.title: Time-to-event data: censoring, Kaplan–Meier estimates and hazard ratios
lessons.worked_example: In the ten-subject table S(5) = 0.9 × 8/9 × 6/7 = 0.6857, S(8) = 0.5486 and the median is 10 months; 12 events in 480 person-months against 20 in 400 gives a rate ratio of 0.50.

lessons.title: Many tests at once: family-wise error, Bonferroni and the false discovery rate
lessons.worked_example: Twenty null tests at 0.05 give FWER 0.642; for ten synthetic p-values, Bonferroni at 0.005 rejects 2 while Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.05 rejects 4, because the fourth-smallest p (0.020) meets its threshold (4/10 × 0.05).

modules.title: Effect sizes, intervals and regression to the mean

lessons.title: Effect sizes, confidence intervals and regression to the mean: reading a result for what it can support
lessons.worked_example: A 1.5-unit difference with SE 0.949 gives a 95% interval (-0.42, 3.42) and d = 0.50; quadrupling n halves SE to 0.474; a first reading of 130 with r = 0.7 is expected to retest at 121 with no intervention.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.
Added an original descriptive-data lesson and a deterministic two-field calculation-and-interpretation practice item. The package remains partial.
Added an original interactive coordinate-plot practice activity with separate pointwise partial credit. The package remains partial.

Added an original lesson on time-to-event data (censoring, a hand-checkable Kaplan-Meier table, median survival, rate and hazard ratios) with five formative items with computed keys and four retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added two original lessons (multiple testing with Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg; effect sizes, confidence intervals and regression to the mean) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

limitations: Four compact legacy units are preserved alongside one supplemental original unit; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.
There is no authored 12–15 week schedule, substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm, cumulative final, or graded integrative project.
The single formative check per lesson does not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery; association with the first lesson objective is provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.
Legacy numerical specifications preserve the prototype's tolerance and optional unit entry; they do not all enforce significant-figure or dimensional checks.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.
The graph exercise checks coordinate placement on author-specified axes; it does not assess axis selection, uncertainty bars, model fitting, or interpretation.
